transcript.text: my tumble dryer is giving off a burning smell?? is it safe to keep using it

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. A burning smell from a tumble dryer needs taking seriously, because dryers are one of the more common causes of house fires. Leave it switched off and unplugged at the wall, and don't run it again until a qualified engineer has checked it, even if the smell seems to go away. 1. Fluff (lint) building up around the heater or inside the air path. This is the most common reason. It gives a hot-dust or scorched-fluff smell, and it's the dangerous one because lint can catch fire.
2. A worn drive belt or a struggling motor. This usually smells like burning rubber, and you often hear a squeal, grinding or rumbling as well.
3. An overheating fault (a stuck thermostat or a problem with the cut-out) or an electrical fault such as a scorched wire or connector. This tends to smell more like hot plastic or 'electrical'. Some checks you can safely do with it unplugged. 1. Pull out the fluff filter in the door opening. If it's a condenser or heat-pump dryer, open the flap at the bottom front and look at the condenser or second filter. If it's furred up with fluff, the air can't flow, the dryer runs too hot, and fluff is more likely to scorch.
3. If it's a vented dryer, look at the hose at the back. Kinks, squashed sections or a hose full of fluff all trap heat.
4. Turn the drum by hand with the door open. If it feels rough or gritty, or the drum turns too freely with no resistance, that points towards the belt or motor side rather than lint. If you find heavy fluff, cleaning it out is worthwhile. But because there's been a burning smell, the fluff that matters most is often inside, around the heater, where only an engineer can safely reach it, so do still get it checked. To help narrow it down: what does the smell remind you of (scorched fluff or dust, burning rubber, or hot plastic or electrical)? And roughly when was the fluff filter last emptied?
ok it's switched off at the wall now?? it smells like singed dust or hair. the filter was very full, not cleaned for a few weeks?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Good, leaving it off at the wall is exactly right. A singed dust or hair smell, plus a filter that was very full after a few weeks, points quite strongly to fluff (lint) as the cause. When the filter clogs, the air can't carry the heat away. The dryer runs hotter than it should, and fine fluff that gets past the filter settles around the heater and scorches. That fits what you're smelling much better than a belt (burning rubber) or an electrical fault (hot plastic). I'm fairly, but not completely, sure of that. The catch is that the fluff that matters most sits inside the machine, near the heater, where you can't safely reach it. So it still needs an engineer to open it up, clear it out and check that the thermostat and overheat cut-out are working properly. Please don't run it to see if the smell has gone. While it's unplugged, these are worth doing, and they'll help the engineer:
1. Clean the door filter fully. Pull the fluff off, and if it's matted, rinse it and let it dry.
2. If it's a condenser or heat-pump dryer, open the flap at the bottom front and take out the condenser or second filter. If it's furred with fluff, rinse it under the tap and let it drip-dry. A clogged one would confirm the airflow was badly restricted.
3. If it's a vented dryer, check the hose at the back for kinks, squashed sections or fluff along its length, and check the outside vent flap. Whatever you find, tell the engineer the filter had gone a few weeks without cleaning and the smell was like singed dust. It points them straight at the heater area and the overheat protection. Going forward, empty the filter after every load. It's the single best way to stop this happening again. Is yours a condenser or heat-pump model, or a vented one with a hose? And was that part clogged too?
it's a vented one with a hose?? the hose is squashed behind the dryer and I can see fluff inside the end of it. I can't get to the outside vent, it needs a ladder. should I just get an engineer?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Yes, get an engineer. With a burning smell it mustn't be used again until a qualified engineer has checked it, whatever you clean in the meantime. A very full filter and a squashed hose with fluff inside it means the hot, damp air had almost nowhere to go. The dryer ran hotter than it should, and fluff that got past the filter will have built up and singed around the heater. That's exactly the singed dust or hair smell you described. I'm fairly confident that's the cause. 1. Open it up and clear the fluff from around the heater, the air path and the fan.
2. Check that the thermostat and the overheat cut-out are working, since it's been running hot. If either has been damaged, that would be the part to replace, but only once they've confirmed it.
3. Look at the vent route. A squashed hose is usually best replaced with a new one that runs short and straight. Tell them the filter had gone a few weeks without cleaning, the hose was squashed and full of fluff, and the smell was like singed dust. That points them straight to the right places. Once it's been given the all-clear, empty the filter after every load and keep the hose free of kinks behind the machine. Those two habits are what stop this happening again.
